papers.title: 4D-TEMPO: Differentiable 4D-STEM ptychography via fast Physics Optimizers
papers.abstract: Electron ptychography recovers atomic structure from 4D-STEM data: diffraction patterns at multiple positions of a scanned probe. Current codes reconstruct an image and read atoms off it, or fit atoms under an $L_1$ loss; neither gives per-atom uncertainty. We propose 4D-TEMPO, a differentiable physical renderer that fits the atoms, the microscope, and the detector directly to the recorded electron counts under a Poisson likelihood. The output is a list of atoms, each a Gaussian primitive with a 3D position, a thermal width, and a model-conditional error bar from the Fisher information. The Fisher information also conditions the solver, gives the dose (electrons per {\AA}$^2$) each parameter needs, and separates calibration from imaging. On a simulated WSe$_2$ bilayer, starting from the published reconstruction, fitted atoms cut in-plane error by a third (3.2 vs. 4.8 pm) and depth error by 40-61% against its 3D peaks. Depth comes from multiple scattering into the dark field, the faint counts outside the direct beam. The two layers, $10\times$ closer than the depth of field, separate; per-atom depth then follows the layer geometry. When the model is well specified, the bars are calibrated (69% of position coordinates within $1\sigma$). On experimental WSe$_2$, fitted atoms predict held-out patterns better than the three published codes we test. With free probe modes where atoms are incomplete, the same likelihood predicts best on all three held-out benchmarks, matches every WSe$_2$ baseline in 5 min against up to 20.5 h, and passes torchslice at its released setting 180$\times$ sooner on PrScO$_3$. Per-atom error bars, planned doses, and fast reconstruction point to low-dose, real-time 3D imaging of beam-sensitive and dynamic materials.

papers.title: The Price of Discovery: Cost-Optimized Detectors for the GUT-Scale QCD Axion
papers.abstract: Grand unification and string theory point to a quantum chromodynamics (QCD) axion with mass between $10^{-11}$ and $10^{-8}$ eV, while heterotic string theory suggests a mass of $0.5-0.8$ neV. We study which laboratory experiment could discover or exclude DFSZ-strength QCD axion dark matter at and above 0.5 neV at the lowest cost, which we estimate from scaling laws calibrated to historical data. We find that a lumped-element detector, building on the ABRACADABRA concept, can do so with demonstrated readout technology; an example is a shielded toroid about 14 m across with a 6 T NbTi magnet, whose magnet and cryostat we estimate at around 120 million Swiss francs (MCHF). If projected readout targets are met, a 5 m toroid at 25 MCHF suffices. We find these designs by optimizing the toroid, solenoid, and core lumped-element topologies under a common cost metric. The toroid emerges as the most promising and cost-effective topology. The optimal field of the toroid detector is far below the 16 T of the proposed DMRadio-GUT design, which would cost nearly twice as much as our optimum. Heterodyne searches with superconducting radio-frequency cavities, with cavity shapes that we optimize for price, cost between about the same as and twice as much as the lumped-element detectors, but require cavities of volumes $\sim50-2000$ m$^3$. We find that nuclear-magnetic-resonance searches (CASPEr) need orders-of-magnitude gains in spin polarization and coherence. We release axionMultiPhysics, an open-source finite-element and multiphysics package for, e.g., magnetoquasistatic and full-wave electromagnetics, superconductors, readout circuits, and mechanics, from which most of our numerical results were obtained.

papers.title: Projected Sensitivity of a Differential Torsion Sensor for Tests of the Weak Equivalence Principle
papers.abstract: Tests of the weak equivalence principle (WEP) are among the most sensitive probes of new long-range, composition-dependent interactions beyond general relativity and the Standard Model. We evaluate the potential of a differential torsion sensor, which combines long mechanical coherence times with optical-cavity readout and common-mode rejection, for laboratory WEP tests and fifth-force searches. For a representative configuration based on an existing prototype, with Be-Ti test masses and 180 days of coherent integration, the projected noise-limited sensitivity to the E\"otv\"os parameter is $\eta\simeq7.5\times10^{-16}$ and $2.4\times10^{-16}$ for signal modulation at 2 and 20 mHz, respectively, below current ground-based torsion-balance limits. For a baryon-coupled Yukawa interaction sourced by the Earth, the corresponding projected sensitivity to the coupling strength is $\alpha\simeq3.1\times10^{-13}$ and $9.8\times10^{-14}$ for ranges $\lambda\gtrsim10^{7}$ m. We identify the modulation scheme, the material contrast, and the source geometry as the main factors that set the projected reach, and the control of systematic couplings as the main experimental requirement for attaining it. These results indicate that differential torsion sensors are a promising platform for future laboratory WEP tests.

papers.title: Design and performance of the front-end readout electronics for LACT
papers.abstract: The Large Array of Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescope (LACT) will complement the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO) with a target angular resolution of 0.05 degrees to resolve the morphology of Very-High-Energy gamma-ray sources. The array is designed to comprise 32 telescopes with 6-meter apertures within LHAASO at an altitude of approximately 4410 meters. Each camera contains 1616 silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). We developed a front-end readout electronics (FEE) board integrating 16 channels of SiPM gain compensation and high-speed waveform sampling for operation at high altitude and over a wide temperature range. The gain compensation circuit independently adjusts the operating voltage of each SiPM according to its temperature and monitors the actual operating voltage. Previous tests of the adopted compensation scheme showed SiPM gain drift below 2% from -20 to 30 degrees Celsius. The waveform sampling circuit uses two 14-bit AC9628 analog-to-digital converters, each operating in eight-channel mode, to digitize the SiPM pulse waveform at 250 million samples per second. The integral nonlinearity of the DC response is 0.0709% over a differential DC voltage range of -950 mV to +950 mV at the AC9628 input. Equivalent electrical pulses with a full width at half maximum of 37.42 ns are used to simulate the SiPM output signals. At a differential pulse amplitude of approximately 237 mV at the AC9628 input, the pulse integral area resolution is 0.2725%. This paper presents the circuit design and performance tests of the FEE for the LACT camera.

papers.title: Producing $\mu$Bq/m3-level low-226Ra ultrapure water for the Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory
papers.abstract: The Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO), a 20 kton low-background liquid-scintillator (LS) detector, was designed primarily to determine the neutrino mass ordering. JUNO requires ultrapure water (UPW) with a Ra concentration < 50~$\mu$Bq/m3 because of the direct liquid-liquid contact between LS and UPW during detector filling. To meet this stringent requirement, a high-sensitivity measurement system capable of detecting Ra in water down to 3.9 $\mu$Bq/m3 was developed, and the 100 t/h UPW production process was optimized. By integrating selective ion-exchange resin with membrane-based separation technologies, the system consistently produced UPW with a Ra concentration of <4$\mu$Bq/m3, exceeding the JUNO specification and, to our knowledge, representing one of the lowest reported levels achieved at this engineering scale. This paper describes the design and implementation of JUNO's UPW system and the high-sensitivity Ra measurement platform, together with a systematic evaluation of Ra removal efficiencies across the purification train and validation of the final water quality.

papers.title: The ALICE asynchronous software trigger processing for LHC Run 3
authors: Sara Pucillo for the ALICE Collaboration
papers.abstract: The detector and computing upgrades for LHC Run 3 enable ALICE to continuously acquire proton--proton (pp) and lead--lead (Pb--Pb) collisions at interaction rates of up to 1.5 MHz and 50 kHz, respectively. The resulting pp dataset is more than three orders of magnitude larger than the combined Run 1 and Run 2 samples, and its long-term retention in full would be impractical given the available storage capacity. To address this challenge, ALICE has implemented a physics-driven asynchronous software trigger designed to retain only collisions containing signals of physics interest. Following full asynchronous reconstruction, the Central Event Filter Processor applies more than 100 analysis-based selection channels spanning the ALICE pp physics programme. The selected collisions are then used to skim the original Compressed Time Frames (CTFs), preserving the relevant detector information within detector-specific time windows. This procedure reduces the retained CTF volume to approximately 4.5% of its original size, while preserving the possibility of future reconstruction with improved calibrations and software. This contribution describes the implementation and operation of the asynchronous software trigger, from collision selection to CTF skimming, and highlights how this strategy provides access to rare signals and processes across the ALICE physics programme.

papers.title: Study of the intra-pixel timing resolution of planar silicon sensors using the TDCpix ASIC
papers.abstract: A study of the intra-pixel timing resolution in planar silicon detectors, bonded to the TDCpix Application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC), is performed using the TimePix4 telescope. Spatial non-uniformities in the timing resolution, arising from the weighting field, are measured for the first time in an experimental environment. The results are validated using simulation and discussed in the context of future Research and Development (R&D) goals.

papers.title: Simulation Study of the MPD Performance for Dielectron Measurements at NICA
papers.abstract: The Multi-Purpose Detector (MPD) experiment at NICA is designed to investigate strongly interacting matter at high net-baryon density through a broad program of heavy-ion measurements. Dielectrons constitute one of the key probes in this program, with contributions emitted throughout the entire space-time evolution of the collision. Their experimental measurement is, however, challenged by a large combinatorial background arising primarily from incompletely reconstructed photon conversions and Dalitz decays of light neutral mesons. In this work, we study the expected performance and capabilities of the MPD experiment for dielectron measurements using simulated minimum-bias $^{209}$Bi+$^{209}$Bi collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 9.2 GeV. Electron identification is performed using the combined information from the TPC, the TOF detector and the ECal. A previously developed multilayer-perceptron classifier is used for electron identification, providing a substantial increase in electron detection efficiency relative to sequential one-dimensional selections while preserving an electron-sample purity close to unity. To address the dominant sources of combinatorial background, a pair-analysis strategy is developed that exploits partially reconstructed electron tracks. The method combines the pair opening angle, the TPC dE/dx signal, and an approximate reconstruction of the pair invariant mass to tag tracks from photon conversions and $\pi^0$ Dalitz decays at the pair level. In the mass interval 0.2 $< m_{ee}<0.7 $ GeV/$c^2$, the method improves the signal-to-background ratio by a factor of about 3.5 with the current track reconstruction algorithm. The study demonstrates the strong potential of the MPD experiment for dielectron measurements at NICA energies and highlights the importance of further improvements in low-$p_{\rm T}$ track reconstruction.

papers.title: Residual diffusion for fine-structure enhancement in low-count accelerator-based muon imaging
papers.abstract: Accelerator-based muon imaging combines the penetrating power of high-energy muons with selectable momentum and a controlled beam direction, offering a powerful means of probing internal structures in large, dense and heavily shielded objects. Within a fixed beam-time budget, realizing this potential requires reliable recovery of fine structures from limited muon statistics. We propose an observation-conditioned residual diffusion method with decoupled linear schedules to enhance low-count muon images through iterative restoration guided by the observed image. We evaluate a simplified VSC-24 fuel cask under an idealized 5 GeV parallel muon beam, using 500,000 accepted events per low-count image and 40 million per reference image. Simulation results show improved recovery of structural boundaries and fine details, with the mean peak signal-to-noise ratio increasing from 11.4239 to 22.1719 dB. These findings highlight the potential of diffusion models to make more effective use of limited muon data and broaden the application of accelerator-based muon imaging across scientific and industrial settings.

papers.title: The Barrel Imaging Calorimeter of the ePIC detector at the Electron-Ion Collider
authors: for the ePIC Barrel Imaging Calorimeter (BIC)
papers.abstract: The Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) is a next-generation facility expected to address fundamental open questions in nuclear physics, including the structure and dynamics of gluons in nucleons and nuclei. The Barrel Imaging Calorimeter (BIC) is the electromagnetic calorimeter of the ePIC detector, designed to meet the stringent performance requirements of the EIC, providing precise measurements and particle identification of scattered electrons, photons, and neutral mesons. The BIC is a high-granularity sampling calorimeter based on lead absorbers interleaved with scintillating fibers, complemented by pixelated imaging layers based on the AstroPix monolithic active pixel sensor. This hybrid design enables both accurate energy and position measurements, as well as three-dimensional shower reconstruction, making it a key component for realizing the full physics potential of the EIC. The BIC has successfully completed its Preliminary Design Review last year and is currently progressing toward the Final Design Review. In this talk, I will present an overview of the BIC concept and focus on its current status and performance results from bench tests, system integration studies, and recent beam tests.

papers.title: Characterization of the fast neutron response of liquid scintillator detectors at NFS
authors: A. P\'erez de Rada Fiol (Centro de Investigaciones Energ\'eticas
G. del R\'io (Universidad Complutense de Madrid)
X. Ledoux (Grand Acc\'el\'erateur National d'Ions Lourds)
papers.abstract: The fast neutron response of MONSTER and sTED liquid scintillation detectors was investigated using time-of-flight measurements at the Neutrons For Science facility at GANIL-SPIRAL2. A continuous neutron beam produced by 40 MeV deuterons on a thick beryllium converter was used to obtain pulse height distributions for selected incident neutron energies. Digital pulse shape analysis was used to distinguish neutron-induced events and reduce pile-up effects. For MONSTER, the response and detection efficiency were studied up to 40 MeV using Geant4 with previously obtained light output functions and PHITS in SCINFUL mode. The comparison examines the increasing importance of carbon reaction channels and the divergence between the calculated efficiencies above 20 MeV. For sTED, light output functions for recoil deuterons and alpha particles were determined for the first time for this detector. The measured and calculated efficiencies were compared up to 20 MeV. The sTED efficiency shows a good overall agreement with the simulations. These results provide experimentally constrained detector response information for nuclear data measurements and identify limitations that must be considered when extending the simulations to higher neutron energies.

papers.title: Depth-enhanced molecular imaging with two-photon oblique plane microscopy
papers.abstract: High-numerical-aperture (NA) oblique plane microscopy enables noninvasive fluorescence imaging of subcellular dynamics without radical sample modification. However, performance degrades at depth in multicellular specimens as scattering and refractive-index heterogeneity raise out-of-focus background. We report a two-photon oblique plane microscope that improves resolution at depth by combining high-NA single-objective detection with multiphoton plane illumination. The microscope achieves $\sim\!300$ nm lateral and $\sim\!650$ nm axial resolution, with single-molecule sensitivity and $<\!60$ nm localization precision in vivo. Compared with two-photon point scanning, the lower illumination NA delivers order-of-magnitude lower peak intensity, enabling $>\!5\times$ faster volumetric acquisition (up to $3.25 \times 10^6$ voxels s$^{-1}$). In multicellular contexts, near-infrared nonlinear excitation enhances contrast throughout the illumination depth by $\sim\!2\times$ and restores volumetric resolving power by $>\!2\times$ relative to linear excitation. We demonstrate these capabilities through molecular imaging of epithelial tissue, stem-cell-derived gastruloids, and living fruit fly embryos, including multicolor transcription-factor dynamics, optogenetic subcellular control, and single-mRNA tracking, all using standard glass-based mounting.

papers.title: Graphene Transfer for Vertical Amorphous-Selenium Photodetectors: Fabrication, Optical Transmission and Operation at 77 K
papers.abstract: Graphene can serve as a VUV transparent electrode in vertical photodetector devices. Using an optically transparent graphene as a top-electrode of amorphous selenium (a-Se) photoconductor requires transfer process compatible with the thermal and chemical sensitivities of a-Se thin films. The baking and polymer-removal steps of conventional commercial Trivial Transfer graphene procedures are undesirable because heating can promote selenium crystallization and prolonged solvent exposure can cause delamination. We implement two alternatives: PMMA-free transfer of nominal 50-layer graphene and transfer of nominal 10-layer graphene using an approximately 80 nm PMMA support removed in acetone at 40C. Raman G and 2D bands identify graphene after transfer. Separate graphene/MgF2 specimens are characterized by dark-corrected transmission measurements over 120-325 nm and compared with earlier single-layer and nominal 6-8-layer Trivial Transfer spectra. The completed graphene/a-Se/Cr devices produce bias-dependent voltage transients under pulsed 415 nm illumination at 293 K and 77 K. These results establish an a-Se-compatible fabrication route for graphene-electrode devices and demonstrate vertical device operation at both room and cryogenic temperatures. The completed devices provide a platform for detection-efficiency studies, and direct VUV photoresponse measurements now underway.

papers.title: Evaluation of tracking plane pitch and xenon-helium gas mixtures for the NEXT experiment
papers.abstract: NEXT is an experimental program to search for neutrinoless double-beta decay ($\beta\beta 0\nu$) in high-pressure xenon gas using electroluminescent time projection chambers. A key feature of the NEXT technology is the reconstruction of MeV-scale electron tracks, which plays a key role in identifying $\beta\beta 0\nu$ events. This work presents a Monte Carlo study aimed at determining the optimal configuration for NEXT detectors employing SiPM-based tracking planes. The simulations are carried out in the NEXT-100 detector geometry, and to classify the events as signal or background, we use a Sparse Convolutional Neural Network. We find that topological rejection power improves by approximately a factor of two at the lower pressure studied (5 bar) compared to the baseline design (13.5 bar). A finer pitch also offers consistent improvement, where reducing pitch from 15 mm to 5 mm decreased the accepted background fraction by a factor of approximately 1.4 at 13.5 bar for a fixed signal efficiency in the different configurations studied. The addition of helium to reduce electron diffusion provides a comparable enhancement, reducing the accepted background fraction by up to a factor of 1.5 at 13.5 bar. We highlight two key practical configurations at 13.5 bar pressure: the present NEXT-100 (pure Xe with a 15 mm tracking plane pitch) and an upgraded NEXT-100 (a Xe-He gas mixture and a 10 mm tracking plane pitch). These results provide quantitative guidance for the design and optimisation of future NEXT detectors, balancing physics performance with technical and financial constraints.

papers.title: Optical readout of MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors with SiPMs
papers.abstract: Scintillation light readout of MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors (MPGDs) is used for imaging and track reconstruction applications including in optical Time Projection Chambers (TPC). Typically, high resolution CCD or CMOS imaging sensors are used and PMTs can be employed to obtain auxiliary timing information. We report on the optical readout of MPGDs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) which enables limited spatial resolution. Arrays of SiPMs were used to read out Gaseous Electron Multipliers (GEMs) and Glass Micromegas amplification stages. Center of gravity reconstruction of hit positions yields a spatial resolution of approximately 1.35 mm for signals shared across multiple SiPMs. High gain of the amplification stage as well as the SiPMs enables good signal sharing and is advantageous for position reconstruction.

papers.title: FPGA-based LQG controller and hardware-in-the-loop simulator implementation for nanomechanical systems
papers.abstract: We present an open-source framework for real-time Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulation on the affordable Red Pitaya STEMlab FPGA platform. The controller implements a discrete-time Kalman filter and Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) for systems with up to three coupled oscillatory degrees of freedom, targeting applications in levitated optomechanics, MEMS/NEMS, and related experimental platforms. Complementing the controller, the HIL simulator provides a~configurable second-order stochastic plant with nonlinear input and output mappings, enabling realistic closed-loop testing under real-time and fixed-point constraints. A MATLAB-based workflow automates model configuration, controller synthesis, numerical scaling, and FPGA deployment without requiring specialized hardware expertise. As an end-to-end demonstration, we present the stabilization of a levitated nanoparticle in a two-dimensional double-well potential, illustrating the complete workflow from model definition and simulation to real-time feedback control. The codebase: https://github.com/TU-Wien-ACIN-CDS/FPGA-based-LQG-and-HIL-simulator-for-nanomechanical-systems
